title: MA Market Dynamics: Special Needs Plans and D-SNPs
summary: Special Needs Plans (SNPs) are a specialized type of Medicare Advantage plan designed for specific populations — dually eligible beneficiaries, institutionalized individuals, and those with severe chronic conditions. D-SNPs for dual eligibles are the fastest-growing segment of the SNP market.

objectives.text: Describe the three types of Special Needs Plans
Explain the coverage and coordination advantages of D-SNPs for dual eligible beneficiaries
Identify the financial alignment opportunity in D-SNPs under FIDE and HIDE SNP models

content_blocks.body: **Special Needs Plans (SNPs)** are MA plans authorized to exclusively enroll (or disproportionately enroll) beneficiaries with specific health or social needs. Congress created SNPs in 2003 to allow tailored benefit design for high-need populations.

**Dual Eligible SNPs (D-SNPs)** serve beneficiaries who have both Medicare and Medicaid — approximately 12 million Americans. D-SNPs coordinate Medicare and Medicaid benefits, reducing the fragmentation that plagues dual eligible beneficiaries.

**Chronic Condition SNPs (C-SNPs)** serve beneficiaries with specific chronic conditions — diabetes, CHF, ESRD, dementia, HIV/AIDS. C-SNPs design specialized benefit structures and care management around the targeted condition.

**Institutional SNPs (I-SNPs)** serve beneficiaries who live in or require care at the level of a nursing facility. I-SNPs enable MA plans to coordinate with long-term care facilities and cover the nursing home population.

Dual eligible beneficiaries are among the highest-need, highest-cost people in the healthcare system — 15% of Medicaid enrollees account for 34% of Medicaid spending. They have on average 7 chronic conditions, high rates of behavioral health and SDOH needs, and historically fragmented care across Medicare and Medicaid silos.

**Fully Integrated Dual Eligible SNPs (FIDE SNPs)** hold Medicare and Medicaid risk under a single contract — truly integrating benefits. These plans have the financial alignment to invest in care management that reduces costs across both payers.

**Highly Integrated Dual Eligible SNPs (HIDE SNPs)** have a lower level of integration — they coordinate benefits but may not hold both payer risks.

CMS is pushing toward greater integration through the **Medicare-Medicaid Integration Program** and state-based agreements, recognizing that integrated financing is essential for improving care for dually eligible beneficiaries.
